items.title: When will Apple have its iPhone 18 Pro release event?
items.content_html:
Apple obviously knows, and perhaps some of its retail staff have at least a clue, but for the rest of us, here's the best estimate of when the iPhone 18 Pro will be announced.

No question, it'll be in September. Apple has held its iPhone launches in October, but since 2011 the only time it has done that was during COVID.

The question is when in September we'll find out the all-important updates and, more than ever this time, the all-important prices. Not to drag this out, the smart money says Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

We've been here before

That's the most probable date that has been recently rumored. It's in the first full week of September 2026, which is also when Labor Day is.

Since 2011 when Apple moved its iPhone launches away from their original announcements in June, the unveiling has been close to Labor day three times. In 2015, 2016, and 2022, and each time Apple has made its announcements on the following Wednesday.

In the 15 years since that move to the last quarter of the year, Apple has launched iPhones on Wednesdays five times. It's launched them on Tuesdays nine times, and on Mondays just once, in 2024.

With the exception of the October launches in 2011 and 2020, every iPhone has been unveiled in the first two weeks of September. The latest date was September 14, in 2021 with the iPhone 13 range.

Then the earliest is a tie between 2016 and 2022, which were both on September 7.

Enough guessing

Despite occasional leaks, we obviously won't know for certain when the iPhone launch is until Apple announces the date. But the company has form on even those invitations, too.

It's a form that seems to be lengthening, too. Back around 2013, it was common for Apple to issue invitations to the launches one week ahead of the event.

Expect another gorgeously-designed invitation like this one from 2025, which will then be studied intently for clues - image credit: Apple

That happened several times, such as in 2015, 2016, 2018, and again in 2021. Then for the iPhone 14 event on September 7, 2022, Apple revealed the date two weeks before with an AR invite.

There was again two weeks' notice for the iPhone 15 in 2023, and the iPhone 16 in 2024.

In fact, from the iPhone 14 onwards, Apple has consistently issued invitations two weeks to the day before the event. That means it is now always during the last week of August that it reveals the date.

Two more dates to watch

So expect the 2026 invitation and event date to be announced on Wednesday, August 26. Expect the event to be on Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

Which just leaves the question of when the new iPhones will be available to pre-order. Typically that happens on the Friday immediately following the event, and that won't be changed because of the unveiling being on a Wednesday instead of a Tuesday.

It might be changed because the Friday is September 11. Apple has avoided doing anything on that date since the World Trade Centers were destroyed on September 11, 2001.

Then Apple isn't likely to delay taking orders by very much, if at all, but it might have to push back shipping dates. Typically buyers start getting their iPhones by the Friday after pre-orders open, and that's also when retail Apple Stores get their first stocks.

For the first time since COVID, though, there are likely to be delays in production. In this case it's because of the global chip shortage, which could conceivably mean a longer than usual gap between launch and shipping.

Or it might be that Apple launches on its usual schedule, but will then take longer than normal to fulfil orders.

That's specifically been rumored for the expected iPhone Fold, but it's possible for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max too.

Then if the invitation date, event date, pre-order and shipping dates aren't enough, Apple looks like it will have one more whole set of dates to look out for. Perhaps because of the chip shortage, Apple is strongly rumored to split its iPhone launch for the first time.

If this is correct, the presumption is that Apple will launch its biggest sellers, the Pro models, first. So the regular iPhone 18 may launch in the Spring instead.

It isn't as likely to get an event, though, so at least there's just the launch, pre-order and shipping dates to wonder about then.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro rumor roundup: 2nm A20 chip, C2 modem, under-display Face ID
items.content_html:
Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is right around the corner, and the rumor mill started earlier than normal. Here's what you need to know.

In 2025, Apple gave its high-end iPhone a major redesign, with the iPhone 17 Pro featuring a distinct pill-shaped camera plateau, an aluminum frame, and a bright orange color option. Inside, the A19 Pro chip bumped up the RAM to 12GB, and the phone even gained a vapor chamber cooling system.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, meanwhile, Apple is expected to deliver a more incremental upgrade, with the only noticeable change likely to be on the front of the device. Smaller Dynamic Island aside, it'll be more of the same design-wise.

However, a new chip production process for the A20 Pro is expected to deliver significant performance improvements. Apple's in-house modems might finally see use in the "Pro" iPhone, and multiple sources suggest a major camera upgrade is in the works as well.

Leakers and analysts alike have made countless claims about the iPhone 18 Pro. Here's everything that's been rumored so far.

iPhone 18 Pro release date rumors

While the rumor mill thinks the base iPhone 18 will arrive in early 2027, the iPhone 18 Pro is expected to arrive in September 2026. To be more specific, an August 2026 rumor claims Apple might announce the iPhone 18 Pro during an in-person event on Wednesday, September 9, 2026.

September 2026 is when we'll likely see the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's U.S. retail employees were allegedly invited to enter a lottery to help organize the event. The choice of an in-person event marks a departure from previous prerecorded product reveals, but the alleged timing is in line with a typical September iPhone event.

In February 2026, it was rumored that the iPhone 18 Pro had entered test production. Based on this alleged testing schedule, and rumors from January 2026 and March 2026, a September 2026 launch date seems almost beyond question.

There have been no rumors of a 2027 release for the iPhone 18 Pro, or any other major deviation from the usual September debut for the Pro models. The consensus among different leakers and analysts is that the iPhone 18 Pro will arrive in September 2026.

Design-wise, the iPhone 18 Pro is expected to offer only a few refinements, relative to the iPhone 17 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro colors, design, weight rumors

In November 2025, a source with a good track record claimed the iPhone 18 Pro would have a more uniform appearance at the back, compared to the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple allegedly wanted to eliminate the two-tone effect by making changes to the processing of iPhone backplates.

Early rumors claimed Apple was testing three colors for the iPhone 18 Pro.

This updated production process is allegedly meant to greatly reduce the color difference between the glass section and metal frame. This should ultimately result in a more seamless appearance on the back of the iPhone 18 Pro.

Also in November 2025, three possible color options for the iPhone 18 Pro were detailed: a coffee color, purple, and burgundy. The leaker, also the same source behind the backplate rumor, said that only one of these colors would make it to production. They said the iPhone 18 Pro would not be offered in black, a claim which resurfaced in April 2026.

However, a February 2026 report from a generally reliable source claimed that the three colors Apple was testing were actually different variants of red. Apple allegedly chose stronger colors for the iPhone 18 Pro, partly because the cosmic orange iPhone 17 Pro was popular in China.

In April 2026, another leaker, albeit with a mixed track record, jumped on the crimson red iPhone 18 Pro bandwagon. The same month, a tech news website claimed it had received a list of all iPhone 18 Pro color options. The list consisted of the following colors: Dark Cherry, Light Blue, Dark Gray, and Silver.

Also in April 2026, leaker Ice Universe shared an image of iPhone 18 Pro camera plateau protectors in the same rumored colors. Similar images were posted in May 2026 by an anonymous account impersonating a now-inactive leaker.

The same month, leaker Sonny Dickson shared photos of iPhone 18 Pro dummy units. Again, the dummy phones point to the same four color options mentioned previously, including Dark Cherry. Sometime later, in June 2026, AI-manipulated images of third-party iPhone cases were shared as part of a sketchy iPhone 18 Pro rumor.

Overall, the rumor mill believes the iPhone 18 Pro will be available in dark red, light blue, silver, and dark gray. However, a June 2026 rumor says the iPhone 18 Pro will inherit the color-changing issue the orange iPhone 17 Pro is known for.

The four colors now said to be for the iPhone 18 Pro. Image credit: Sonny Dickson.

In terms of design, the iPhone 18 Pro will maintain the aesthetic of the preceding iPhone 17 Pro. This is per an October 2025 post from the same leaker behind the November 2025 color and backplate rumors. Reports from December 2025 and January 2026 reiterated this claim, while a February 2026 rumor said Apple wasn't changing the design because the iPhone 17 Pro was a hit.

The source behind the February 2026 claim, a Weibo leaker with a mixed track record, then added yet another detail. In July 2026, they said the camera plateau of the iPhone 18 Pro would be 2mm thicker than that of the iPhone 17 Pro. They also said Apple would continue to use aluminum for the casing of the iPhone 18 Pro.

This aligns with what analyst Jeff Pu claimed in January 2026: that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature an aluminum frame, and the same 6.3-inch display size as the current iPhone 17 Pro. In May 2026, however, one leaker suggested Apple was exploring a return to titanium for its high-end iPhone models, while another disputed this claim.

The rumor mill is not in agreement about the iPhone 18 Pro backplate design, either. While a November 2025 rumor said Apple wanted to reduce the two-tone effect, one tipster, with a relatively poor track record, claimed Apple would make the glass backplate stand out even more.

A September 2025 Weibo rumor strangely suggested that Apple would use "slightly transparent" back glass in the iPhone 18 Pro. If implemented, this would have offered a clear view of the MagSafe charging coil, but the design choice has always been an unlikely option.

Images of alleged MagSafe-equipped iPhone 18 Pro cases were shared in May 2026. Supposedly, Apple plans to revert to its earlier case design, meaning iPhone 18 Pro cases will feature a MagSafe ring rather than a solid rectangle on the back. These could very well be third-party accessories, though, so it's unclear if Apple altered the iPhone 18 Pro case and backplate designs.

As for weight, one Weibo leaker says the iPhone 18 Pro will be the heaviest iPhone ever. In November 2025, the tipster suggested the iPhone 18 Pro may be 10g heavier than the iPhone 17 Pro. This would place the iPhone 18 Pro Max weight at approximately 243g (8.57 ounces).

If this rumor is true, the iPhone 18 Pro Max might be the heaviest model ever made. The current heavyweight is the iPhone 14 Pro Max at 240g, while the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs slightly less at 233g.

Though the iPhone 18 Pro has a chance of weighing more, it might actually offer a reduced version of an existing hardware feature. According to an August 2025 rumor, Apple has simplified the Camera Control on the iPhone 18 Pro to save on production costs.

Meanwhile, an earlier report from the same month, though from a leaker with a less-than-stellar track record, said that Apple would remove the Camera Control entirely from its 2026 iPhone lineup.

It's possible that Apple tested iPhone 18 Pro configurations with and without a Camera Control button. The company did exactly that with the iPhone 16 range, and this prototyping approach would explain the seemingly contradictory rumors.

Though we'll have to wait and see what Apple has in store for the Camera Control, multiple leakers agree that a major change is coming to the front of the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro to have punch-hole camera & under-display Face ID

If the rumor mill is to be believed, Apple has been experimenting with the idea of under-display Face ID for years. In January 2023, it was rumored that the technology would be available with the iPhone 16 Pro, echoing April 2022 and April 2021 claims made by analyst Ming-Chi Kuo.

Images supposedly showing a smaller Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro. Image Credit: Early Apple Leaks/Ice Universe

However, the expected timeline for under-display Face ID shifted in March 2023, when DSCC analyst Ross Young said that the technology would not arrive until at least 2025, due to "sensor issues." Meanwhile, a December 2023 report from a different publication said the hardware was actually delayed until 2026.

In May 2024, Ross Young corroborated the rumor of an apparent delay to 2026, reiterating the idea a year later as well. The same month, May 2025, saw the resurgence of under-display Face ID rumors for the iPhone 18 Pro, this time from a Weibo leaker, who reiterated their claims shortly thereafter.

This tipster then went on to repeat the under-display Face ID rumor in June 2025, September 2025, October 2025, and November 2025. Mere days later, however, the Weibo leaker behind the repeated under-display Face ID claims said Apple had delayed the hardware to 2027.

A month later, a completely unknown leaker challenged this alleged 2027 debut date. Tipster "Smart Pikachu" claimed in December 2025 that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature an under-display Face ID system after all.

The same month, a different publication explained it was also expecting the iPhone 18 Pro to debut with Face ID sensors under the display. Apple allegedly wants to "eliminate" Dynamic Island, which the publication calls an "unsightly black oval." Per the report, Canadian company OTI Lumionics will supply the necessary components.

In January 2026, Jeff Pu said he expects the iPhone 18 Pro to offer a smaller Dynamic Island, with Face ID still present. Pu also believes the iPhone 18 Pro will offer an 18MP front-facing camera and a 6.3-inch display. A Weibo leaker said the same thing in January 2026.

The same month, however, YouTuber Jon Prosser added confusion to the mix. He claimed that, with the iPhone 18 Pro, the Dynamic Island would move to the top left side of the screen. This was then disputed in January 2026 by a Weibo leaker with a mixed track record.

Meanwhile, also in January 2026, leaker Ice Universe shared the alleged dimensions of the Dynamic Island on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. Per the leaker, Apple plans to reduce the Dynamic Island by 35% from 20.76mm to 13.49mm on the iPhone 18 Pro Max.

In February 2026, a generally reliable source explained they also expect the iPhone 18 Pro to feature a smaller Dynamic Island. However, a source with a mixed track record claimed in March 2026 that Apple would only decrease the size of the Dynamic Island with the iPhone 19 Pro.

Even so, March 2026 is when the first images of the purported smaller Dynamic Island began popping up. Ice Universe and a relatively unknown leaker, who goes by "Easy Apple Leaks," both shared alleged photos of the iPhone 18 Pro Dynamic Island.

The latter of the two leakers would then go on to share alleged CAD images of the iPhone 18 Pro Dynamic Island in May 2026. All of the images shared so far show the Dynamic Island at the top of the screen, in the center, rather than on the left.

Also in May 2026, a Weibo leaker with a questionable track record said the iPhone 18 Pro would not get a tandem OLED display. Apple will likely continue to use 6.3-inch LTPO OLED panels with ProMotion support for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Given the number of rumors we've seen regarding under-display Face ID, and the frequency with which they appear, there's a decent chance the technology will arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro. It looks as though Apple will indeed shrink the Dynamic Island as well.

If Apple moves forward with the new design, it would increase screen real estate to nearly 98%. Still, a smaller Dynamic Island was rumored to appear with the iPhone 17 Pro in February 2025 and July 2025, but that obviously never happened.

Rumors are still rumors, after all, but the iPhone 18 Pro has a higher chance of receiving Dynamic Island and Face ID modifications. Still, Under-display Face ID is not the only camera-related change rumored for the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone 18 Pro could have a variable aperture camera

As with the smaller Dynamic Island, a variable-aperture camera system was expected to debut with the iPhone 17 range, per a July 2024 rumor. However, in November and December of the same year, Ming-Chi Kuo suggested the technology would, instead, debut with the iPhone 18 lineup.

The iPhone 18 Pro could debut with a variable aperture camera system.

Variable aperture system claims appeared again in an October 2025 report. It listed LG Innotek and Foxconn as the component manufacturers, with an actuator to drive the aperture movement supplied from Luxshare ICT and Sunny Optical.

A Weibo leaker corroborated the rumor the same month. They added, however, that the iPhone 18 Pro's 48MP Telephoto lens, which uses a periscope lens system, will also gain a larger aperture.

In December 2025, another report claimed the iPhone 18 Pro would gain a new aperture system, though it was referred to as a "mechanical aperture" in the text.

Relatively obscure leaker "Smart Pikachu" claimed in January 2026 that the iPhone 18 Pro would feature a variable camera system. They also said Apple was planning to introduce a DSLR-like teleconverter, increasing the focal length and zoom of the iPhone 18 Pro camera system

In February 2026, it was again rumored that the iPhone 18 Pro would gain a variable-aperture main camera, with a larger aperture for the Telephoto lens as well.

According to a supply chain report, production for the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture components began in April 2026. The report claimed that China's Sunny Optical and Luxshare ICT would make the actuators, with LG Innotech also being part of the camera production process.

Rumors of a variable aperture camera system continued through April 2026. The addition of a variable aperture might allow for better night-time photography, while preventing washed-out colors on daytime photos.

Variable aperture cameras have other benefits as well. There are multiple reasons why Apple might use a mechanical, variable aperture system rather than a fixed one.

Smartphone cameras typically feature a fixed aperture, which is the hole that lets light through between the lenses and the sensor. This is the case because a variable aperture would require more physical space for the mechanism and motor.

When aperture size is increased or decreased, this affects the amount of light that hits the sensor. It also impacts the exposure triangle, the principle that changes to the aperture, shutter speed, and sensitivity of the sensor can influence how a shot is taken.

A wider aperture allows for a shallower depth of field, keeping the subject in focus while blurring the background and foreground. A smaller aperture, meanwhile, facilitates a larger depth of field effect, with more elements in the picture being sharp and in focus rather than blurry.

Apple's current workaround for the fixed aperture limitation is to use multiple camera views and computational photography effects to create a blurry background, known as bokeh, for portraits. However, adjusting the aperture would result in creating a naturally focused image without any computational photography.

Overall, it's practically guaranteed that the iPhone 18 Pro will feature a variable camera aperture system, unless you take into consideration earlier rumors related to the iPhone 17 Pro, which doesn't feature the hardware.

As for other camera components, a July 2024 rumor suggested that Samsung would provide image sensors, instead of the usual supplier, Sony. January 2025 saw the resurgence of this claim, though from a different leaker who added more detail.

Samsung allegedly wanted to make a stacked image sensor consisting of three layers: a photodiode, a transfer layer, and a logic layer.

In essence, the sensor would come with a processor directly mounted to it. This would reduce the time necessary to get image data to the processor, ultimately improving the camera's responsiveness in the process.

In August 2025, Apple announced it aimed to spend $100 billion on manufacturing facilities within its U.S. supply chain. Among the beneficiaries was Samsung.

A report in December 2025 then said Samsung was gearing up to install manufacturing equipment at its Taylor, Texas, factory. This is allegedly where the CMOS image sensors (CIS) used in the iPhone 18 range will be made.

However, there's evidence that Apple won't exclusively use Samsung-made image sensors in the iPhone 18 Pro.

In June 2026, AppleInsider analyzed more than 630GB of internal files taken from Apple supplier Tata in a cyberattack on its factory in India. Our findings suggest that the Wide sensor, or the main rear camera of the iPhone 18 Pro, will switch from the Sony IMX-903 to the IMX-905.

It looks as though Sony will still produce image sensors for the iPhone 18 Pro, though this does not contradict the prior variable aperture system rumors.

As for the front-facing camera of the iPhone 18 Pro, a February 2026 rumor from the obscure leaker "Apple Club" says a 24MP image sensor is planned. Earlier, in January 2024, Ming-Chi Kuo similarly said the iPhone 17 range would feature a 24MP front camera.

These two rumors can be explained away by Apple's use of pixel binning for the front camera. Pixel binning involves averaging the light values of pixels based on the pixels nearby. In essence, the iPhone considers groups of pixels as a virtual "superpixel" of sorts.

Ultimately, Apple's iPhone 17 range delivers 18MP images with the front-facing camera, and this will likely continue with the iPhone 18 lineup.

Potential camera-related improvements aside, the iPhone 18 Pro will almost certainly deliver a performance boost, thanks to Apple's A20 Pro chip.

iPhone 18 Pro performance: 2nm A20 chip, WMCM chip packaging process

In September 2024, Ming-Chi Kuo said that the iPhone 18 Pro would be the only device in the iPhone 18 lineup equipped with a 2nm chip. Back in June 2022, TSMC revealed it would launch its 2nm chip process in 2025, so it makes sense for Apple to go with it for the iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple's A20 Pro chip will most likely use a new packaging process.

Kuo, however, changed his expectations for the iPhone 18 range in March 2025, suggesting that 2nm chips would be used across the iPhone 18 line. This idea aligns with an earlier July 2024 report.

One source suggested, in April 2025, that 2nm chips would lead to a price increase for the 2026 iPhones, with Apple passing the costs on to end consumers. Months later, a November 2025 rumor from a separate Weibo leaker raised similar concerns.

A January 2026 supply chain rumor said the A20 Pro may cost as much as $280 per unit, approximately 80% more than the previous generation. In July 2026, it was similarly alleged that TSMC had increased its base prices by 10%, again hinting at an iPhone price hike.

Prices were already raised across the Mac and iPad lines in June 2026, but the iPhone was left untouched, for now. Jeff Pu said in July 2026 that the iPhone 18 Pro might cost users $250 to $300 more than the iPhone 17 Pro, after previously saying in February 2026 that there would be no price increase with the model. Counterpoint Research similarly suggested a $200 price increase in July 2026.

In any case, while a price hike appears to be right around the corner, performance improvements will arrive with it, in the form of 2nm chips. The A20 Pro system-on-chip is expected to offer a performance boost of between 10% and 15%, relative to the current iPhone 17 range, according to an October 2024 report.

Per the report, the A20 Pro chip utilizes a new packaging method known as WMCM, rather than Apple's current packaging technique, InFo.

Chip packaging represents a process applied to the die of a chip, setting it up to communicate and work with other components on a circuit board.

With the A19 Pro chips, the InFo process gives Apple a way of integrating components within a chip package. Essentially, elements like memory can be added to the chip package directly, rather than being an externally accessed component.

This lets Apple make the overall chip package quite small. Still, it is a technique that's used with a single die. New CPU and GPU combinations require new dies with this method, which could become expensive for Apple.

WMCM, short for Wafer-level Multi-Chip Module, is a different packaging technique that works well with multiple dies. It can fit together separate dies, such as a CPU and GPU, while still keeping the overall package extremely small.

Switching to WMCM would give Apple more freedom to create multiple packaging designs by incorporating different dies, and it wouldn't massively raise the cost of making the dies themselves. Using WMCM wouldn't have a massive impact on performance, but it would reduce reliance on chip binning for different product tiers.

Apple's alleged plans to use WMCM have been mentioned by multiple sources, and our own findings also suggest next-generation iPhone chips will use this packaging process.

Jeff Pu revealed in June 2025 that he also believes the iPhone 18 range will use a 2nm chip with the WMCM process. He reiterated these claims in January 2026. According to Pu, the process the A20 Pro will use is referred to as N2 and is a first-generation process.

Silicon chip wafers. Image Credit: TSMC

The smaller die has the potential to make the A20 Pro chip approximately 15% faster than the A19 Pro. It might also be more efficient, with a 30% reduction in power consumption. Apple's use of the WMCM packaging process was also suggested in a December 2025 report.

Additionally, an April 2025 rumor claimed that the iPhone 18 line would feature 6-channel LPDDR5X memory. This would ultimately allow for improved memory bandwidth, thereby enhancing performance. The use of LPDDR5X memory was corroborated in an October 2025 report, which added that it would be sourced from Samsung, though SK Hynix and Micron were reportedly in talks with Apple as well.

Per a similar December 2024 report, meanwhile, Apple worked with Samsung to change how RAM is packaged, also in an attempt to increase bandwidth.

Additionally, iPhone 18 Pro board schematics seen by AppleInsider in June 2026 suggest the system-on-chip will move closer to the outer edge of the dual-layer board. The storage of the device will seemingly sit deeper between the two board layers, which could impact repairability and performance.

The same month, leaker Ice Universe spotted a detail about the A20 Pro Neural Processing Unit or Neural Engine. This area of the chip is seemingly much larger than that of the A19 Pro Neural Engine, suggesting Apple will prioritize additional on-device processing for Apple Intelligence and Siri.

While every iPhone 18 Pro will feature the A20 Pro chip, Apple might take a different approach with the phone's cellular hardware.

iPhone 18 Pro modem configurations and battery rumors

In June 2026, AppleInsider exclusively revealed that Apple had developed two logic board variants for the iPhone 18 Pro. One of them features a Qualcomm modem and supports mmWave; the other is equipped with Apple's C2 modem.

The iPhone Air already uses an Apple modem, so it makes sense for the C2 to arrive with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In short, our findings suggest that iPhone 18 Pro units sold in the United States will use a Qualcomm modem, while devices sold elsewhere will use the Apple C2 modem.

Jeff Pu also claimed in January 2026 that the C2 would be used in the iPhone 18 Pro. Identifiers for the C2 modem were also discovered in July 2025, within an early build of iOS 18, while a February 2025 rumor claimed new Apple modems were in the works.

The same month, Apple's SVP of hardware technologies, Johny Srouji, referred to the C1 modem as "a platform for generations." Ultimately, it's not surprising that Apple has plans for the C2 modem.

We believe the iPhone 18 Pro will offer region-based configurations, with some users getting the C2, and Qualcomm modems being available for U.S. buyers, due to mmWave compatibility.

As for battery life, a February 2026 rumor says the iPhone 18 Pro battery capacity will only be slightly larger than that of the iPhone 17 Pro. Then in June 2026 and July 2026, it was claimed the iPhone 18 Pro battery would have a 4,288mAh battery in the United States, and a 4,056 mAh battery in China.

For reference, the U.S. version of the iPhone 17 Pro has a 4,252 mAh battery, while the model for the Chinese market has a battery capacity of 3,988 mAh. Models sold in China have a lower capacity because the physical SIM card slot takes up space in the phone, which is not the case with the eSIM-only U.S. models.

If the February 2026 numbers are correct, the iPhone 18 Pro sold in the United States will offer a battery capacity increase of only 0.85%. The China-specific physical SIM model would offer a similarly meager 1.71% improvement over the iPhone 17 Pro.

Battery enhancements aside, one thing we won't see with the iPhone 18 Pro is MagSafe replacing USB-C entirely, as TikToks in February 2026 strangely suggested. The iPhone 18 Pro will obviously continue to feature MagSafe and USB-C, as dummy units posted in April 2026 clearly indicate.

What to expect with the iPhone 18 Pro

In essence, the iPhone 18 Pro could deliver the following enhancements and changes over the preceding iPhone 17 Pro:

  • Under-display Face ID
  • Punch-hole front camera
  • Variable aperture system for rear cameras
  • 15% faster, 2nm A20 Pro chip with improved memory bandwidth
  • New red, blue, silver, and gray colors with a unified color scheme
  • A $200 to $300 price increase

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is expected to arrive in September 2026, likely alongside the long-rumored iPhone Fold.

items.title: Still simple, still powerful, BBEdit is a Mac app legend
items.content_html:
You may like Pages and you may tolerate Microsoft Word, but text editor BBEdit has been rightly earning devotees on the Mac for 34 years. Here's how.

There are very few Mac apps that go back this far, and even fewer that remain both actively developed and actually beloved by its users. And there is only one with the trademark "It doesn't suck."

BBEdit is just a text editor, but rather than this meaning it is limited, it means that BBEdit is focused. It is and always has been a plain text editor, it does not also try to be a mind-mapping tool or an image editor or a chatbot.

This is going to read like an unqualified hymn of praise, although there are actually a few qualifications. But this is what BBEdit does to you. While there are other apps I write in for many different purposes, BBEdit does what it does extraordinarily well.

I don't remember when I first came across it, but it would've been before 2000 and possibly before Steve Jobs came back to Apple. Its original version was written in 1989 because of a problem with editing text on the Mac.

After it was released as BBEdit in 1992, Bare Bones Software never stopped developing it.

The problem back then was just that Apple offered an API for handling text, but it couldn't handle large files. The creators of BBEdit were working on a version of the Pascal programming language for Mac that effectively demanded longer files.

While Apple's Pascal faded away, their text editor grew into this favorite for programmers and writers.

If you've never used it, though, it's hard to convey just why BBEdit is so popular among its users. There are people who will never leave the Mac because there isn't a PC version of BBEdit, for instance.

And as you use it, you have such a clear sense that so do its developers. This is not a day job or a side project, BBEdit keeps getting better because its developers add what they want it to do themselves.

"I use BBEdit for everything I produce that involves text: code (C, C++, Objective-C), web site content (HTML, Markdown, Textile), and more," said Rich Siegel, developer of the app, in a 2011 interview. "In a very real sense, BBEdit is written using itself — my daily-use build is the same one that's being beta tested or used in the field by our customers."

If BBEdit's search feature can't find something, it isn't there.

So an app that has been available for more than three decades, two hardware architectures ago, is still being actively developed. An app that was meant to be just a "bare bones" text editor is still simple to use, yet it has so many features a keystroke away that it's hard not to gush about this app.

To be fair, there are actually reasons not to use it, there are writers for whom BBEdit is just the wrong choice. But if it suits your writing or it suits how you like to work, BBEdit can make you into a passionate fan.

"BBEdit is legendary because we keep improving it to serve the needs of our customers," Siegel said on the release of version 9. It's now on version 16, which is promoted as having "millions* of new features and refinements (*estimated)."

With marketing like that, BBEdit remains a taste of those early times with the Mac some 34 years after it was first launched. It's serious software that doesn't take itself too seriously.

What BBEdit does and how

The short version is that BBEdit is a text editor. That's not the same thing as a word processor which offers formatting options like styles or margin control, as a text editor is just for getting the words down.

There aren't countless settings you can choose in BBEdit, but there are more than you'd like to count.

As such a text editor, BBEdit is fast and responsive, and it generally doesn't get in your way. You don't have to set any settings, you can just open it and start typing.

When you have written a lot of text, maybe even over several years, you will start to appreciate a feature called grep. This is a form of regular expression, the feature takes you beyond normal search and replace.

For instance, in any word processor you could search for a date like 01/12/2026. But in BBEdit, you can search for all dates in the document, matching every one of them simultaneously.

It's a form of regular expression. As well as being powerful, though, the BBEdit version includes an on-screen guide to help you through it as simply as possible.

"Our base started as Mac software developers, scientists, system administrators, and other technical users," Rich Siegel told Apple in 2019. "The first big change was popularity among HTML authors and web back-end developers."

Web designs can write CSS files in BBEdit - image credit: Bare Bones Software

"As word spread, we were able to help folks understand that the internet was built with text that you could treat as data or you could treat it as a document," he continued. "So the next wave brought in internet architects, cryptanalysts, and scientists from unexpected disciplines."

Thos unexpected disciplines, he said, included "writers and other content creators-folks who see their text not as data but as words, and who want as little as possible between them and their words."

Overall design

Beyond the simplicity of writing in BBEdit, part of this get-on-with-it design is in how it stores your documents. Unlike most apps other than Ulysses, BBEdit can in theory be a single repository for all of your writing.

So rather than opening and saving documents all the time, you can just open BBEdit, press Command-N and be writing in a new document. Everything you've written before is still there, listed in a navigation bar on the left, until you choose to close it.

You don't even have to save that previous work before you start a new one.

But then if you want to, you can. Anything you write can remain in BBEdit's list on the left of the screen, but you can also save any of it out to separate, individual .txt files.

You can keep all of your recent documents open in BBEdit. Or don't even ever save them, just write in this text editor and export the final text to wherever you need it to go.

Then it might not require you to set anything up, and it might not get in your way, but BBEdit is built to help you. So for example, if you type an opening quote mark, BBedit immediately adds a closing one right after it and leaves your cursor in the middle.

It's the same with brackets. Type an opening bracket, and you get that plus a closing one for free. That's chiefly convenient in that it means you can't ever forget to include a closing speech mark or bracket, you'd have to choose to delete them.

If you're a programmer, that can also make the difference between your code working or not. It's easy to forget to close brackets, unless you're writing in BBEdit.

But it is also a little pain when you're writing dialog. So often you're going to follow a speech with a phrase like "she said," and to do that you have to cursor over the automatically-inserted end quote mark.

You can set BBEdit to wrap words and it also supports Markdown, plus a split-screen view.

You may well have just shrugged at that, and if you did, it's because you are the true target audience for BBEdit. While any type of writer can use it, and every type of writer does, it is best for coders and programmers.

These are people whose writing tends to be in short lines rather than paragraphs. So they may never even need to notice something about BBEdit lines that will strike a novelist or a journalist immediately.

That's how, by default, BBEdit does not wrap text at the end of the screen or at some margin stop. You could write a novel on the same long single line if you wanted to.

But then you could alternatively go to Settings, Editor Defaults, and turn on Soft Wrap. Set it to wrap your text at a specific character count, at the width of your default page size for printing, or the width of the window.

There are hundreds upon hundreds of settings you can change, but none that you have to in order to start writing. You can readily believe the gag that it has "millions" of new features, but this is still not an app where you have to study the manual.

Although, actually, there is a manual. In another throwback to the early days of the Mac, there exists to this day a 456-page BBEdit manual, and it is constantly updated.

How it got here

BBEdit began as this way to address a problem on the Mac. Today you know TextEdit as the name of Apple's free text editing app, but back in the day, it was what the company called its text handling API.

If you wanted to include text in your app, from a word processor to just labels on a drawing, you could use this API and it did the job. But it wouldn't handle anything over 32K, it wouldn't handle anything long.

BBEdit was made to show that longer files could be handled on the Mac. It did the job, it was popular, and in 1992 when it first came out, BBEdit was also free.

As well as automatically adding closing brackets for any user, if you're a programmer or web designer then BBEdit will offer auto-completion suggestions - image credit: Bare Bones Software

That didn't last. Around a year later, Bare Bones Software launched version 2.5 and began selling it for $99 (around $230 in today's money). Users of the previous free ones, or owners of various programming languages such as THINK Pascal, could buy it for $49.

At the same time, Bare Bones Software released a cut-down edition called BBEdit Lite. That was free, and users of it could upgrade to the full BBEdit for $49.

They could get it on a floppy disk by mailing — not emailing, regular postal mailing — the developer on an Massachusetts address. Please enclose a check for $5.

BBEdit Lite no longer exists, and nor does its brief replacement, TextWrangler. That was released in 2003 for $49, offering what Bare Bones Software thought would be a compelling mix of BBEdit features for programmers and database administrators.

Compared to some apps, TextWrangler did well, sticking around 14 years, even if it quickly became free. It may have seemed like it spent much of that time nagging users to upgrade to BBEdit, but come 2017, there was no longer any choice.

TextWrangler was ostensibly folded back into BBEdit and users were encouraged to move to the full app.

"We promise that you will feel right at home, because BBEdit and TextWrangler are identical in every way that you're used to," said the company at the time. "They're built on the same foundation, by the same developers, with the same care; and they work the same way."

Behind the scenes, that must've been a reason to drop TextWrangler. Maintaining the same code base across two apps was surely taking up time that could be spent developing new features.

It certainly wasn't the lure of cash from upgraders that made Bare Bones Software do this. As welcome as that would doubtlessly be, the company also sweetened the deal.

If you bought or upgraded to BBEdit at that time, you could use it for free for 30 days. It's not unusual to have such a trial period, but what happens afterward is much more rare.

Bare Bones Software made it so that you could continue using the app for free, with just a limited feature set. What it left in was generous, and really it created what was effectively a new, free, BBEdit Lite in all but name.

BBEdit and Apple

If you're a long-time Mac user, you may distantly remember technologies such as OpenDoc, but you're unlikely to have used any of it. Bare Bones Software has, it even added OpenDoc support to BBEdit.

BBEdit has been a good Mac citizen from the start but sometimes you don't know what you've got until it's gone. That happened with Apple and BBEdit over the Mac App Store.

While it's never really seen a fraction of the business that the iPhone App Store has, the Mac version has been around longer than you think. It debuted in 2011 and BBEDit was right there as one of the very first products on the Mac App Store.

By 2014, though, it was gone.

The reasons given at the time were not very specific, but they centered on how the Mac App Store sandboxes apps. Any app on the store is deliberately limited to prevent it being able to control the user's Mac or other apps.

In BBEdit's case, the app was reportedly not allowed full access to the user's files and folders. It needed to be able to open and save wherever the user wanted, and at the time, Apple put limits on this.

There was also, though, an issue of money. While BBEdit was a one-time purchase, Bare Bones Software has always issued paid upgrades at intervals.

The Mac App Store did not allow for paid upgrades once a user had bought the app. So the company could have gained a true believer but never know it, never profit from it, and that user would never know what new features were available.

By 2019, enough developers had complained about sandboxing that Apple made some changes. They were sufficient to mean that BBEdit came back on the Mac App Store, but perhaps chiefly because there was now a solution to the upgrade problem.

Apple welcomed BBEdit back to the Mac App Store with a trio of promotions - image credit: Apple

While Apple still does not allow paid upgrades, it both allows and encourages subscriptions. So today you can buy BBEdit 16 from the developer for a one-off $60, but you can subscribe via the Mac App Store for $5/month, or $50/year.

And if you were looking when BBEdit returned to the Mac App Store in 2019, you will have seen Apple rushing to make up for arguably ignoring it. That return saw an App Store front page profile of its main developer, Siegel, plus an article about BBEdit's search features, and another about its overall feature set.

At that time, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing was Phil Schiller, who oversaw the App Store. He tweeted a welcome back to BBEdit, although that tweet is no longer available since Schiller quit Twitter/X back in 2022.

There's something missing

BBEdit sounds perfect. Unless you're a novelist or a screenwriter, or perhaps even a non-fiction author, maybe it is. And if you are any of those things, you can make BBEdit work for you if its comprehensive yet no-nonsense feature set appeals.

What you can't do is make BBEdit work on anything other than a Mac. There's no PC version, for example, although if you cared about that you wouldn't be reading this far into an AppleInsider article.

The real missing piece is the iPad.

It's been some years since Bare Bones Software has talked about why it's stayed Mac-only. So perhaps things will change, but 37 years after starting it, and 34 since it went on sale, BBEdit is a legend among macOS apps.

Enough so that it's one of the very, very few apps I would enthuse about this much. Bare Bones Software and Naomi Pearce helped out with finding images like that ancient photo of the boxed version, but they haven't read this prior to publication, and they certainly didn't pay for it.

Try it out for yourself. Once again, it may not be the right writing tool for you, but if it is, you'll become a fan.

BBEdit 16 for Mac is available for $60 direct from the developer as a one-time purchase. You can also get it from the Mac App Store on subscription for $5/month, or $50/year.

attachments.title: Still simple, still powerful, BBEdit is a Mac app legend

items.title: Apple continues to dominate premium smartphone market share in 2026
items.content_html:
For smartphones selling at over $600, Apple owns 65% of that market and grew 9% year over year in the first half of 2026. However, Chinese brands are making a dent in local market share.

Apple ships 23% of all smartphones sold globally and captures 49% of all profit. It's a behemoth on its own, but when accounting for smartphones in the $600 plus range, it's the clear leader in market share.

According to a report from Counterpoint Research, Apple captured 65% of the global premium smartphone market. It grew 9% year over year during the first half of 2026, though its market share is still down when compared to the 74% held in 2022.

The decline since 2022 can be attributed to the premium Chinese smartphone market growing in popularity. When a Chinese consumer is presented with an option between an iPhone and a smartphone from Huawei, Xiaomi, or Oppo, they choose the local brand.

That said, Apple still holds most of the market globally at 65% and Samsung at 19%. The other OEMs make up the remaining 16%.

Apple holds onto 65% of premium market share even as the rest of the market increases prices. Image source: Counterpoint

The premium smartphone market grew 5% overall year over year for the first half of 2026 and makes up a record 29% of the global market. The global RAM shortage driving up prices has pushed more smartphones into the premium $600 plus segment and price hikes on lower-end models are driving customers to more premium models.

The report suggests these trends are why smartphone manufacturers are leaning further into financing options. Samsung recently launched its Galaxy Card while Apple has introduced Apple Upgrade.

Trade-in prices have also gone up, as was seen with Apple earlier Thursday. Everything is meant to entice customers holding onto their more expensive devices for longer to upgrade sooner in spite of price increases.

It's going to be an interesting fall as everything seems to be creating quite the hurdle for Apple to overcome. iPhone 18 Pro sales could be limited by the RAM shortage and Apple reports that it's already selling as many iPhone 17 models as it can make.

Demand won't be the issue, but supply held back by global supply chain instability. Consumers may be feeling the impact of economic uncertainty, but that may not matter if financing options continue to be plentiful.

items.title: Jon Prosser's baby forces another extension to Apple's legal battle
items.content_html:
Jon Prosser was sued by Apple over the alleged theft of pre-release information, saw a default ruling due to inaction, had that overturned, and is once again failing to provide discovery materials. There's a reason this time.

Life hasn't been easy for Jon Prosser since a July 2025 lawsuit from Apple accused him and Michael Ramacciotti of stealing information from Apple employee Ethan Lipnik's test device. He says he's not guilty, but has created roadblocks at every possible point in this case.

According to a new filing, Jon Prosser has not been responding to requests for discovery since he rejoined the case in June. Apple last heard from Prosser's counsel on July 6, 2026.

In the interim, Prosser had a second child. The lack of response is attributed to the newborn.

He allegedly hasn't had time to provide requested materials. In the filing he says that he "will find dates when additional discovery may be provided to Apple."

However, given the situation involves a newborn, Apple appears to be a little more understanding of this delay. The joint filing suggests that Apple has approved the delays in discovery and the new dates.

What isn't clear is whether Apple will take a softer approach to the final determination and punishment for Prosser. The worst case here is that he is barred from reporting on Apple, which is a significant portion of his business.

A new deposition is set to take place in September 2026. The next legal filing is expected on October 7, 2026.

items.title: New ChatGPT version has a 'Think' button, will find 'more reliable facts'
items.content_html:
OpenAI continues to churn out upgrades to its various GPT models, the latest GPT-5.6 promises to be more succinct and provide confident wrong answers less often. Here's what's new.

Apple and OpenAI have a relationship where ChatGPT is an extension for the previous version of Siri, though that could come to an end soon. The latest updates don't affect users of that specific function, but the Mac utilities and iOS app will gain new features and performance.

Now, we're going to have to sift through OpenAI's anthropomorphized language of its chatbot models to understand exactly what's being introduced here. The press release says a lot about "thinking" versus instant answers, but always remember: artificial intelligence can't think, reason, understand, or sympathize.

GPT-5.6 Sol appears to be a release hoping to address several concerns brought up by users of ChatGPT. They often complain it uses too many filler words, takes too long to get to the point, and provides affirming answers even when the user is wrong.

ChatGPT caveman

According to the release, GPT-5.6 Sol provides "more focused answers, adapts its level of detail to the question, avoids unnecessary formatting, and offers a helpful correction when simply agreeing wouldn't be useful." These problems have become so well known and bothersome users have turned to skills like "caveman" to force ChatGPT to be brief and direct.

SiriAI gets to the point, while OpenAI does shows some restraint

The example provided by OpenAI looks incredibly similar to what a user might see when using Siri AI. A brief summary of a weather result with a weather widget is shown instead of a wall of text padded with filler.

Incredibly, the release mentions "more reliable facts." Hallucinations are a part of AI no matter how many guardrails are introduced, so it'll be interesting to see if OpenAI has actually accomplished this in a meaningful way.

For example, Siri AI tends to avoid hallucinations by not summarizing content when possible. When you ask a question, the source is quoted and linked directly, which ensures random incorrect information isn't inserted. Of course, that's only if the answer is correct in the first place.

While AI tools can be used for research, AppleInsider strongly urges users to avoid any AI-generated content from appearing in a finished work. Lawyers, doctors, and financial advisors have encountered horrific problems when relying too heavily on AI to perform their work.

No amount of promises and fixes from OpenAI will create a foolproof AI tool.

A "Think" button

If you've used Siri AI, you might notice that the same question can sometimes produce very different results in terms of detail. That's because on-device models are much smaller and seek an end result that is much less computationally expensive versus server-side models.

Apple and ChatGPT have similar ideas on how to approach AI chatbots

Apply that same idea to ChatGPT "Thinking" and Instant modes, and you'll understand what's happening. Previously, these two models would be so different that the answers would vary wildly in tone or style.

The names say what they do: Thinking takes longer with a heavier model while Instant is fast with a smaller model. There's also a new "thought" slider.

This terrible naming convention is yet another attempt to humanize the chatbots, but basically, think of it as a compute slider. Lower means less compute, faster results, while higher means more compute, longer, more detailed results.

Obviously, OpenAI hopes users will change the slider for more simple queries that don't need a lot of information resources. It's computationally less expensive, uses less tokens on input, and likely means less tokens on output.

That's likely going to be useful for private ChatGPT use, but corporate users never bother. Research shows that OpenAI's most expensive ChatGPT users are in an office, choosing the most complex GPT version available, and doing so to convert a PDF into a slideshow.

It's wasteful and expensive, especially for OpenAI, which is likely giving that compute time away at a bargain. Sliders would be helpful for the company that can't turn a profit, but not if users just ignore them.

Free GPT

Free users are also getting an upgrade as everyone will default to GPT-5.6 Luna and gain a "Think" button for questions users believe are harder.

AI is a tool that is now easily found on your iPhone, which is a problem for OpenAI

Analyzing such an update can provide interesting insight into OpenAI. It's priorities as a company providing AI to the masses while developing a HomePod that can wiggle is interesting. Especially given the Apple lawsuit.

One of the biggest reasons why OpenAI has such a large valuation is because it released a powerful technology and essentially gave it away for free. Like Spotify, the free use of this technology is draining the company and all that keeps them afloat are whales and investors.

The AI bubble is teetering on collapse, or is at least deflating, even as consumers tire of AI as a concept. It isn't clear if OpenAI will find its footing before it runs out of cash sometime in 2028, or if everything comes crashing down around it.

As an Apple fan, the whole thing is a train wreck observed in real time. Sure, it took two years for Apple to find the right path forward with AI and execute that plan, but it spent pennies on that compared to its competitors.

items.title: OpenAI's new hardware leaks: Over $300, same size as an Alexa Dot
items.content_html:
Details have leaked about OpenAI's new hardware, and by all accounts, it's going to be shaped and sized a lot like a second-generation Alexa Dot, be battery-powered, and retail for between $300 and $400.

The rumor mill has been loaded with rumors about OpenAI's hardware. A new accounting of the device says it will be a smart speaker without a display.

Furthermore, it is rumored to be about the same size as a hockey puck, like the second-generation Echo Dot pictured above, and donut-shaped. It is also said to include parts that will move on their own, to assist with responding to a user. Somehow.

According to a report by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, OpenAI expects users to use the device as an AI assistant during the day, similar to ChatGPT voice on the iPhone. It is expected to have more advanced models, but what that means isn't clear.

Like the Echo family of products, it is expected to learn about the user over time.

Like the HomePod, and as expected for a voice AI assistant, the device will have speaker grills and microphones for conversation. Most importantly, perhaps, and setting it apart from the HomePod, it will be battery-powered, and maybe able to be used hand-held.

But it is expected to have a camera to feed visual information into ChatGPT, or whatever OpenAI calls the model on the device.

Thursday's report cites sources familiar with the matter in saying that the device will refute allegations of abuse of Apple's trade secrets. It's not entirely clear how, given that the same sources say the device will have upscale materials and high-quality metal.

OpenAI is said to have investigated Apple's IP use in this product with an internal probe following the lawsuit. It's only been four weeks since that suit was filed, on a Friday. That assessment timeline feels very quick for a complete technology stack assessment of a product which is apparently close to shipping.

Similar assessments over Samsung's smartphone design in that omnibus trial with Apple took months to complete.

And, presumably, that high-quality metal has to be finished. A highlight of the first filed legal document by Apple launching the suit is allegations of theft of a metal finishing technique. A different donut-like shape certainly doesn't preclude the possibility of IP theft.

The device in question is said to have been designed in collaboration with LoveFrom. Notably, Jony Ive, founder of LoveFrom, has not been named in the OpenAI IP theft suit.

And the device is supposed to launch a new line of devices. Release dates aren't clear for this product, nor any other hardware shipping from the company.

items.title: Apple issues another round of macOS security updates as patch frequency increases
items.content_html:
Apple has rolled out another round of security updates for macOS Tahoe, macOS Sequoia, and macOS Sonoma.

Thursday's update is the second round of macOS updates to be released in less than two weeks. According to Apple, the patch solves an issue with Screen Sharing. The patch note reads, "An attacker on the network may be able to authenticate to Screen Sharing without valid credentials."

Apple says that the issue was addressed with improved state management.

The release builds are as follows:

  • macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, build number 25G76
  • macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, build number 24G830
  • macOS Sonoma 14.8.9, 23J631

How to update your Mac

  1. On your Mac, click the Apple Menu
  2. Click System Settings
  3. Click Software Update
  4. If available, click Update Now or schedule an update with Update Tonight

AppleInsider, alongside Apple, suggests that you download the update as soon as is convenient. These kinds of updates are critical for patching vulnerabilities and keeping your devices performing optimally.

This may be the new normal

If you believe Apple is releasing security updates more frequently than it has in the past, you are correct. Apple has gone on record saying that they will no longer wait to include updates in upcoming scheduled releases.

The company intends to further cut the time between discovery of an exploit and the update to address it. This is the same reason we saw the iOS 26.5.2 update in late June.

items.title: Adobe is hell-bent on becoming the creative engine behind AI
items.content_html:
Adobe's newest AI ChatGPT plugin shows that the company doesn't care where people create, but more on ensuring they create with Adobe.

On Thursday, Adobe and OpenAI rolled out a new feature. A new ChatGPT tool that would combine more than 70 of Adobe's creative tools into a single plugin, accessible by typing @Adobe.

If you've got an Adobe account, you can go to ChatGPT, install the Adobe plugin, and begin generating... Well, whatever you want, really.

For example, you could type:

@Adobe Create a 16:9 hero image of a robot artist working over a drawing desk or at a computer. Give it a vaporwave paper collage aesthetic. It should feel lightly foreboding.

And you'd get something like the image above.

It's an interesting tool, primarily because it doesn't just generate images. You could make short videos or even PDFs thanks to its Acrobat integration.

Currently, anyone can use this for free. Both paid ChatGPT and paid Adobe accounts offer more expansive features.

The benefits for OpenAI are numerous, obviously. The company wants to turn ChatGPT into a one-stop shop for everything from creative output to medical triage.

But what's in it for Adobe?

While the all-in-one plugin is new, it's not Adobe's first plugin for ChatGPT. Before, you could install individual plugins that allowed you to use a single tool, like Photoshop at a time.

And Adobe doesn't just partner with OpenAI. There is an Adobe Photoshop plugin for Anthropic's Claude, with Google Gemini and Slack versions set to release in the future.

I suspect that Adobe will eventually package this all-in-one plugin for other platforms, too. Adobe's all in on AI; that much is clear.

As always, it's worth taking a little time to look at how we got here.

Adobe, everywhere.

For decades, Adobe has stood atop the digital creative software mountain without many competitors. This allowed the company to become industry standard in many fields.

Even smaller, independent artists usually found themselves beholden to Adobe. At least until they were priced out and forced to seek alternatives.

Hell, Adobe even influenced the vocabulary around image manipulation. For years, everyone referred to seemingly unbelievable images as "being Photoshopped."

Though now I suspect we'll hear that term replaced with "that's AI." It's already being wrongly thrown about as an excuse why a reader doesn't like something that's been written by a human, so why not?

Its reign as creative king gave Adobe incredible power in the space. When competitors like Affinity and Procreate peeled off the smaller, independent artists, Adobe knew that it could weather the storm because it had the industry money.

Unfortunately, that's not the case anymore. Some of it is Adobe's fault, to be clear.

At the time of publication, Adobe stock has lost nearly 60% of its value in the past five years.

Adobe's pricing practices and cancellation flows are, to put it lightly, abhorrent. So much so that the Department of Justice had to step in.

Coupled with aggressive price increases, Adobe's burnt through the last of the goodwill it had built up with artists. Many people have decided that Adobe's products, good as they may be, aren't worth it anymore.

But, it's not entirely Adobe's fault, either. Some of it is the market Adobe is forced to operate in.

The creative industry, and especially the commercial sector, has been restructuring for years. Instead of having full-time staff, many corporate creative jobs are now per-project, and rely heavily on small teams of independent contractors.

This means that Adobe doesn't get to rely on a fat paycheck from a large corporation buying hundreds of full-ride software license packages.

The problem becomes compounded, again, when the creative industry finds ways to cut ties with the artists who long held it up. Artificial intelligence is being used to reduce the number of working artists even further, which could directly affect Adobe's bottom line as well.

Unless...

No, really: Adobe everywhere.

I've spoken at length about Adobe's rush to embrace AI several times. As a person who has been using Adobe products since about 2001, I can say that this was probably inevitable.

And, while I don't agree with it, I get it. For the first time, possibly ever, Adobe's on the back foot.

Not only is it dealing with an industry that is feeding itself into a wood chipper, but it also has actual competition in products like Canva. This is especially true in relatively young markets like social media platforms.

Adobe needs to find its place again, or the company risks facing the same layoffs and restructuring that plague the rest of the tech industry. By selling subscriptions to ChatGPT users, Adobe may be able to buy itself a little breathing room.

Eric Shinseki, a retired United States Army general who served in senior roles under Presidents Clinton, Bush, and Obama, once said, "if you don't like change, you're going to like irrelevance even less."

Adobe knows this. It probably doesn't love the idea of hocking subscriptions to users of another service.

Unfortunately, if you've built your livelihood in an industry cannibalizing the very creative labor that made it, adapting may mean becoming bedfellows with the technology threatening to replace you.

items.title: OpenAI fires back, says Apple is suing because it can't compete
items.content_html:
ChatGPT maker OpenAI wants Apple's lawsuit dismissed, calling it "rotten to the core" and a pretext for how the firm is failing in AI and at keeping its staff.

While Apple went back to court to ask that its lawsuit against OpenAI over alleged trade secret theft be sped up, OpenAI initially turned to the court of public opinion. But it has now responded to Apple's latest filing with one of its own, presented to a US judge with the request that the case be dismissed.

According Reuters, the filing first denies Apple's claims of trade secret theft by arguing that it is not making anything that would benefit from such theft. "OpenAI has no use, need or desire for Apple's trade secrets," says the filing. "OpenAI is building something entirely new and different from anything at Apple."

The filing first denies Apple's claims of trade secret theft by arguing that it is not making anything that would benefit from such theft.

"OpenAI has no use, need or desire for Apple's trade secrets," says the filing. "OpenAI is building something entirely new and different from anything at Apple."

The filing then goes on to more specifically say that Apple's case "fails to sufficiently describe the information for which it claims trade secret protection." It even says that Apple has failed to prove that it owns "a protectable trade secret," or to "plausibly allege misappropriation" by OpenAI.

Apple does unquestionably have trade secrets, though. And while OpenAI says Apple has only listed "generalized product development categories," it would be unlikely to reveal any further detail in filings that were always going to be made public.

Apple's real reasons for suing

Having sought to downplay Apple's allegations, OpenAI's new filing then sets out to present itself as the blameless victim of Apple's failures.

"Apple should not be permitted to use a baseless and pretextual lawsuit to make up for its shortcomings in the market for talent and retaining its employees," continued the filing, "and its failures to integrate AI into its products."

Returning to its repeated insistence that messages prove its employees only helped Apple, OpenAI says that the company is trying to spin the facts. Instead of ex-Apple employee Tang Tan keeping confidential documents, the "opposite is true and at least equally plausible."

"Mr. Tan retained this information to help ensure that new employees coming from Apple followed Apple's offboarding procedures and did not retain any Apple confidential information," says the filing.

Cherry-picking arguments

This entire matter is an IP theft suit. They are historically messy, and loud. And, lawyers want to argue their own points.

So, this is of course a completely expected filing. Apple has sued, OpenAI wants the case dismissed or at least wants a future trial to see that it believed it had reasons for dismissal.

It may have those beliefs, but based on what has been published so far, this latest motion still ignores key parts of Apple's accusations. Specifically, it appears to concentrate on the issues surrounding ex-Apple vice president Tang Tan and whether he retained documents.

"Apple tries to spin Mr. Tan's possession of the offboarding document as evidence of an attempt to evade confidentiality obligations," the filing claims. "The opposite is true, and at least equally plausible: Mr. Tan retained this information to help ensure that new employees coming from Apple followed Apple's offboarding procedures and did not retain any Apple confidential information."

The original filing does not "spin" Tan's possession of the offboarding document as anything more than still he has the offboarding document. The OpenAI filing does not address the actual claim about the document, that Tan did not complete off-boarding and dodged attempts to have it done.

And, while Apple does accuse Tan of this, the company names several other ex-employees, including Chang Liu. Apple alleges that Liu retained his Apple-issued laptop, which OpenAI's recent blog posting seems to confirm, and that he downloaded confidential files.

Then OpenAI's initial statements that it is building something "entirely new" that has no resemblance to anything Apple has made could be problematic. Leaked information appears to show that the first OpenAI hardware device will be a smart speaker that is much like Apple's HomePod.

But OpenAI had to try. It decided to use the same criticisms that have been leveled against it over cherry-picking messages to refute accusations.

"Plainly filed without adequate investigation and built on selectively excerpted communications and ordinary conduct stripped of context," concludes OpenAI's new filing, "Apple's complaint is — to borrow its own phrase — 'rotten to its core.'"

Regardless of what OpenAI or Apple wants or feels, the case is unlikely to be dismissed at this juncture. Consequently, it seems unlikely that a judge will agree to a dismissal. Claims that Apple hasn't done enough investigation seem transparently false, as the company clearly has server logs of access and downloaded records.

No court dates have been set beyond an October 1 hearing on Apple's injunction and early discovery request. Barring a settlement, this suit is likely to wear on for years, not unlike Apple vs. Samsung, or Epic vs. Apple.
